newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland seeks place on NATO-Russia council.
newsitem.headline: Poland seeks place on NATO-Russia council.

text.p: Poland welcomed Wednesday's deal between Russia and NATO on peaceful cooperation and said it would now seek some form of representation on a new council to be set up by Moscow and the Western military alliance.
"Poland welcomes the agreement..., which is a basis for cooperation and lowering tensions in Europe," Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati told reporters.

"It (the deal) removes one of the important elements of dispute.... Although the calendar of NATO expansion would have been implemented regardless of the agreement, it will now proceed in a better climate, a better atmosphere," he added.
In remarks reported by PAP news agency, Rosati said Poland would seek a presence on the Russia-NATO council to be formed after the signing of the deal expected on May 27 in Paris.

"I think it is natural that on such a Council, on the NATO members' side, some form of presence should be foreseen for those countries who aim to join the alliance in the not-distant future," PAP quoted him as saying. @
NATO has promised to invite a first batch of countries which once belonged to the defunct Warsaw Pact to start talks on membership at a summit in Madrid in July.
Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary, leaders of economic and democratic reforms in eastern Europe, are expected to be among the first invitees.
Rosati said the deal, struck in Moscow by Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana, should not infringe on the rights of new NATO members.
"The agreement should not create a second-class membership category and must in no way provide for delaying the alliance's expansion," he said.

Poland's Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, visiting Sweden, earlier said he was concerned that Poland should be able to exert at least as much influence on NATO policies as Russia would have, as it negotiated to join the alliance.
"From my point of view it can be a kind of paradox that a country that is not going to join NATO, like Russia, may get a stronger position in relation to NATO than applicant countries," he said.

Details of the agreement, now submitted for consideration to NATO governments and to Russian President Boris Yeltsin, were not immediately released and it was not clear if all differences had been fully resolved.

Rosati said Poland had so far been consulted at all stages of the negotiations and had no reasons for disquiet, but would seek full information on all aspects of the agreement as soon as possible and before it was signed on May 27.
